He governs (yuqaddir) the affair, deciding and ordaining it according to what wisdom requires. If you ask: what is the position of this clause? I say:

The preceding clause has already indicated the greatness of His station and His sovereignty through the creation of the heavens and the earth, despite their vastness and extent, in a short time, and through His istiwa' (settling) upon the Throne. He followed it with this clause to add further indication of His greatness, and that no matter of any affair goes outside His decree and ordainment. Likewise His saying ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾ is evidence of His might and majesty, like His saying ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, they will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to what is known by that greatness, that is, that Great One described by these attributes is ﴿your Lord﴾, the One who deserves worship from you. So ﴿worship Him alone and do not associate with Him any of His creatures, whether a king or a human, let alone a lifeless thing that neither harms nor benefits﴾. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ For even minimal reflection and contemplation would alert you to the error in what you are upon. ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾, meaning that in the final outcome you will return only to Him, so prepare yourselves to meet Him.

﴿The promise of Allah﴾ is an absolute infinitive (mafʿul muṭlaq, a verbal noun in the accusative used for emphasis) confirming His saying ﴿to Him is your return﴾, and ﴿truly﴾ (ḥaqqan) is an absolute infinitive confirming His saying ﴿the promise of Allah﴾.

﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes) whose meaning is to give the reason why the return to Him is necessary. Is it true, servants of God, that I come not, nor go, except that a watcher is over me?

Originally: "And if God were to hasten evil for people as He hastens good for them," so He placed their seeking of good hastily (istiʿjaluhum bi-l-khayr) in the place of His hastening good for them, indicating the swiftness of His response to them and His granting their request, so that their seeking of good is as though it were His hastening it for them. The intended people are the people of Makkah. Their saying, "Rain down upon us stones from the sky" (Qur'an 8:32), means: if We were to hasten for them the evil they called for, just as We hasten good for them and grant them what they ask, then "their term would have been decreed for them" (laqudiya ilayhim ajaluhum), meaning they would have died and been destroyed.

It has been read as laqudiya ilayhim ajaluhum with the verb in the active voice, the agent being God, the Mighty and Majestic; and the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) supports it: laqadayna ilayhim ajalahum ("We would have decreed their term for them").

If you ask: how is His saying "So We leave those who do not expect meeting Us" (Qur'an 10:11) connected to this, and what is its meaning?

I answer: His saying "And if God were to hasten" implies the negation of hastening, as if it were said: "We do not hasten evil for them, and We do not decree their term for them; so We leave them in their transgression," meaning: We grant them respite and pour blessings upon them despite their transgression, as a way of establishing the proof against them.

in the accusative of state (ḥāl), as shown by the conjunction of the two states after it, meaning: He calls upon Us lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. If you ask: what is the benefit of mentioning these states? I say: its meaning is that the one afflicted by harm does not cease calling, does not slacken in supplication until the harm leaves him. So he calls upon Us in all his conditions: if he is prostrate, unable to rise, weak in getting up [[Commentary note: "unable to rise": nahada nahdan wa nuhūdan: stood up. (G)]] [[Note: "weak in getting up": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: nāʾa yanūʾu nawʾan means he rose with exertion and hardship. (G)]], or he is sitting and cannot stand, or he is standing and cannot bear walking, and the one who is distressed, until he becomes completely relieved, and health and full radiance (al-mashah) are restored to him. [[Note: "al-mashah": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "upon so-and-so is a mashah of beauty." (G)]]

It is also permissible that what is meant is that among those afflicted some are in a worse state, namely the one confined to bed; others are lighter, namely the one able to sit; and others are able to stand. All of them cannot do without supplication and seeking the removal of calamity. For man, as a species, passed on, i.e. continued on his earlier way before the touch of harm, and forgot the state of hardship. Or he turned away from the station of supplication and humble entreaty and does not return to it, as if he had no acquaintance with it: ﴿as if he had never called upon Us﴾, as if he had not called upon Us. The word is lightened and the pronoun of the matter is omitted. The poet said:

*"And a bright chest — as if its two breasts are two caskets..."*

That is: "And many a chest..." (some narrate it in the nominative, as a conjunction with something mentioned earlier, meaning "and she has..."). The chest (naḥr) is the place of the necklace on the breast. Another narration reads: "and a bright breast," i.e. white and shining; another: "and a bright-chested breast"; another: "and a bright-faced face," and *kaʾanna* is a lightened form of the heavy one, whose noun is the pronoun of the matter. Abū Ḥayyān said: there is no need for an implied pronoun when it is left unparsed. It is also narrated as *kaʾanna thadyayhi* with the verb in the dual with lightening, which is rare. The attachment of the two breasts to the pronoun of the chest is by way of association, and to the pronoun of the face by way of an assumed omitted noun, i.e. "the two breasts of his companion." *Ḥaqqān* is the dual of *ḥaqq*, which is made of ivory or the like, in which the most precious things are placed. It is said to be the dual of *ḥaqqa*, with the feminine *tāʾ* removed.

﴿Thus was made attractive to the extravagant﴾ — the like of that adornment was made attractive to the wasteful: the Shaytan made it attractive by his whisperings, or Allah by abandoning them and leaving them to themselves, ﴿what they used to do﴾ — of turning away from the remembrance and following desires.

The phrase لَمَّا is an adverbial of time governing أهلكنا ("when [We destroyed them]"). The waw in وَجاءَتْهُمْ is a circumstantial (حال) waw: they did wrong by denying, while their messengers had already come to them with the proofs and evidences of their truthfulness, which are the miracles.

As for His words وَما كانُوا لِيُؤْمِنُوا, they may be coordinated (عطف) with ظلموا, or they may be a parenthetical clause (اعتراض). The lam in لِيُؤْمِنُوا emphasises the negation, meaning: "they would not truly have believed," as an affirmation of the negation of their faith, and that God knew of them that they would persist in their disbelief, and that faith was improbable from them.

The meaning is that the cause of their destruction was their denial of the messengers, and God knew that there was no benefit in granting them respite after the messengers had established the proof against them. كَذلِكَ, "in the same way," refers to that recompense, namely destruction: نَجْزِي كُلَّ مُجْرِمٍ, "We recompense every criminal." This is a warning to the people of Makkah for their criminality in denying the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

It has been read as يُجزى with the yaʼ.

ثُمَّ جَعَلْناكُمْ: the address is to those to whom Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, meaning: We made you successors (استخلفناكم) in the land after the generations that We destroyed, لِنَنْظُرَ, "so that We might see," أتعملون خيراً أم شراً, "whether you will do good or evil," so that We may deal with you according to your deeds.

كَيْفَ is in a position of accusative (نصب) governed by تعملون. It does not take the preceding verb (لا ينتظر) because the sense of interrogation in it prevents its governing verb from preceding it.

If you say: how is "looking" (النظر) permissible for God, when it implies confrontation (المقابلة)? I say: it is used figuratively for certain knowledge, which is knowing a thing as existing, likened to the looking of one who looks and the direct witnessing of one who witnesses it in its being established.

[Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: I used to think that al-Zamakhshari would limit himself to denying the servant's seeing of God, but he added to that the denial of God's seeing, and combining these two errors is the doctrine of a group of the Qadariyya, who say: God is neither seen nor sees. Exalted is God far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation. The refutation of their claim that seeing entails confrontation and corporeality has already been given earlier, so we will not repeat it, and God is the Granter of success.]

The Qur'an's condemnation of idol worship and its warning to the polytheists enraged them, so they said: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, one that does not contain what angers us about these things, and we will follow you; or change it.﴾ That is, make a verse of punishment into a verse of mercy in place of a verse of punishment, and drop the mention of the gods and the condemnation of their worship. So he was commanded to answer regarding the change, because it falls within a human being's power: to put a verse of mercy in place of a verse of punishment among what has been revealed, and to remove the mention of the gods. As for bringing another Qur'an, that is not within human capacity. ﴿It is not for me﴾ means "it is not fitting for me, nor lawful for me," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say﴾ [7:116 is cited in the sense of the same wording]. ﴿To change it on my own accord﴾ means from my own self. It is also read with a fatha on the ta': [[The phrase "min ghayr" here is perhaps meant as "ay min ghayr" (i.e., "that is, without"). (ʿ)]] without my Lord commanding me to do so. ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾: I neither add nor omit anything of that kind except by following the revelation of God and His commands. If a verse is abrogated, I follow the abrogation (naskh, abrogation); if a verse is substituted for another verse, I follow the substitution. It is not for me to substitute or to abrogate. ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord,﴾ by substituting or abrogating on my own, ﴿the punishment of a great day.﴾

If you say: did it not become apparent and clear to them that they were incapable of producing the like of the Qur'an, so that they said, "Bring a Qur'an other than this"? I say: Yes, but they did not acknowledge their incapacity, and they used to say, "If we willed, we could say the like of this" [8:31], and they said, "He has invented a lie against God" [cf. 6:21], attributing it to the Messenger while claiming that he was able to produce it and its like, even though they knew that the Arabs, despite the abundance of their eloquent and articulate speakers, when they were unable to produce it, each individual among them was even more incapable.

If you say: perhaps they meant, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it, from the direction of revelation, just as you brought the Qur'an from its direction." And by his saying, "It is not for me," he meant: "it is not easy for me, nor within my ability, to change it." I say: His saying, ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾, refutes this.

If you say: then what was their purpose, when they were the most cunning of people and the most cunning in this proposal? I say: deceit and guile. As for the proposal to replace a Qur'an with another Qur'an, it implies that it is from you, and that you are able to produce its like, so replace it with another. As for the proposal of substitution and alteration, it arises from greed and from testing his condition. And if any alteration were found in him, either God would destroy him, and they would be rid of him, or He would not destroy him, and they would mock him and make the alteration an argument against him and a confirmation of their claim that he had fabricated against God.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 16:

﴿Had God willed, I would not have recited it to you﴾. He means: its recitation is only by the will of God and His bringing into being a wondrous matter outside of customary habits, namely that a man who is unlettered, who had not studied, had not listened to or observed scholars for an hour of his life, and had not grown up in a land where there are scholars so that he could read to them a book of eloquence that overwhelms every eloquent speech and rises above all prose and poetry, filled with knowledge of the sciences of the foundations (usul) and the branches (furu') of law, and reports of what has been and what will be, speaking of the unseen matters that none knows except God. He had lived among you for forty years, while you observed his circumstances, and nothing of his secrets was hidden from you, and you had not heard from him a single letter of this, nor had any of those nearest to him and closest to him known it from him; ﴿nor would He have made you know it﴾, nor would He have informed you of it through my tongue. Al-Hasan recited: ﴿wa-la adra'tukum bihi﴾ (nor would He have made you know it), in the dialect of those who say a'tahu and arda hu, meaning a'taytuhu and ardaytuhu. The recitation of Ibn 'Abbas supports it: ﴿wa-la andhartukum bihi﴾ (nor would I have warned you with it). It was also transmitted by al-Farra' as ﴿wa-la adra'tukum bihi﴾, with a hamza. In this there are two possibilities. The first: the alif is changed into a hamza, as it is said: labba'tu bil-hajj, ra tha'tu al-mayyit (I lamented the dead), and halva'tu al-sawiq (I made the porridge sweet), because the alif and the hamza are from one root. Do you not see that when the alif is touched by vowel movement it turns into a hamza? The second: that it comes from darra'tuhu when I pushed him away, and adra'tuhu when I made him a repeller, meaning: I did not make you, by its recitation, adversaries who repel me with argument and call me a liar. From Ibn Kathir: ﴿wa-la-adrakum bihi﴾, with the lam of beginning, to affirm the act of making known; its meaning: had God willed, I would not have recited it to you, and He would have made you know it through the tongue of another than me, but He bestows His grace upon whom He wills of His servants, and He singled me out with this honor and deemed me fit for it over all other people. ﴿So I had dwelt among you a lifetime﴾; it was also read as ʿumuran with sukun. He means: I remained among you as a youth and as a mature man, and you did not know me to be engaged in anything of this kind, nor was I capable of it, nor was I one described as possessing knowledge or eloquence, so that you might accuse me of inventing it. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ so that you would know that it is only from God and not from one like me. This is the answer to what they slipped beneath their saying: "Bring a Qur'an other than this," in attributing fabrication to him.

"Who is more wrong than one who invents a lie against God?" The phrase "one who invents a lie against God" may mean the invention of the polytheists against God in their saying that He has a partner and has offspring, and it may be that it is a rejoinder to the fabrication they attributed to Him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 18:

﴿What neither harms them nor benefits them﴾: the idols, which are inanimate objects that have no power to benefit or harm. It has also been said: if they worship them, they do not benefit them, and if they abandon worshipping them, they do not harm them. It is the right of the worshipped that it should reward obedience and punish disobedience. The people of Ta'if worshipped al-Lat, the people of Makkah worshipped al-Uzza, Manat, Hubal, Isaf and Na'ila, and they used to say: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾. It is related from al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, al-Lat and al-Uzza will intercede for me." ﴿Will you inform Allah of what He does not know?﴾: will you inform Him of their being intercessors with Him? This is information about something that is not known to Allah. And if it is not known to Him, while He is the Knowing in essence, encompassing all things known, then it is not a thing, because a thing is that which is known and about which information is given. So it is information with no object of which it informs. If you say: how did they inform Allah of that? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verses 19–20:

"And mankind was not but one community [united upon ḥanīfiyyah (pure monotheism)], agreeing upon one religion (millah) without disputing among themselves. And that was in the time of Adam until Qabil (Cain) killed Habil (Abel). It was also said: after the Flood, when God left none of the disbelievers upon the earth as dwellers (diyār)." ﴿And had it not been for a word that had already preceded from your Lord﴾ — namely, the deferral of judgment between them until the Day of Resurrection — ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾ immediately concerning that about which they differed, and the true would have been distinguished from the false. The preceding of His word with deferral was for a wisdom that required this abode to be a place of obligation (taklīf), and that abode a place of reward and punishment.

And they said: ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ They meant a sign of the kind they were proposing. They did not regard as significant the great and abundant signs that were sent down to him, the like of which were not sent down to any of the prophets. The Qur'an alone suffices as a lasting sign upon the face of time, wondrous and unique among signs, subtle in its method among the miracles. Yet they regarded its descent as no descent at all, as though no sign had ever been sent down to him, to the point that they said: "Why has not one sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" This was due to the extremity of their obstinacy, their persistence in rebellion, and their absorption in error.

﴿So say: "The unseen belongs only to God"﴾ — that is, He alone is the one specially knowing the unseen, which He has kept exclusively to Himself; neither I nor anyone else has knowledge of it. The meaning is that what prevents the sending down of the proposed signs is a hidden matter that none knows but Him. ﴿So wait; indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ — for what God will do to you because of your obstinacy and your denial of the signs.

Allah sent famine upon the people of Makkah for seven years, to the point that they were nearly destroyed. Then He showed them mercy with rain. But when He showed them mercy, they began to revile the signs of Allah, to oppose the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to plot against him. The first "idha" (when) is conditional, and the second "idha" is its answer, and it indicates suddenness (al-mufajaah). Al-makr (scheming) means concealing deceit and keeping it hidden, taken from a woman who is "mamkurah," meaning her frame is folded and concealed. The meaning of "massathum" (touched them) is that it mingled with them until they felt the evil effect of it upon them.

If you say: the verse does not describe them as quick in scheming, so how is "asra'u makran" (quicker in scheming) correct? I say: Indeed, the word of suddenness indicates this. It is as if He said: when We show them mercy after harm, they suddenly commit scheming and hasten to it before they have washed their heads from the touch of harm, and they do not wait the time it takes to swallow their throat-morsels. The meaning is: Allah, exalted is He, has arranged your punishment, and He will inflict it upon you before you have arranged how you will act to extinguish the light of Islam. "Inna rusulana yaktubun" (Indeed Our messengers record) is an announcement that what you suppose to be hidden and concealed is not hidden from Allah, and He will take vengeance upon you.

It is also recited as "yamkurun," with the ta' and the ya'. It has been said: their scheming is their saying "we were watered by such-and-such a star (nawʼ)." From Abu Hurairah: Indeed Allah makes a people wake up with a blessing and evening with it, and a group of them wakes up disbelieving in it, saying: "We were rained upon by such-and-such a star." [[Narrated by Ishaq, al-Tabari, and al-Tha'labi through the chain of Ibn Ishaq from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Yamani from Abu Salamah from Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah makes His servants wake up with a blessing or evening with it, and a group wakes up with it disbelieving, saying: 'We were rained upon by such-and-such a star.'" Muhammad said: I mentioned the hadith to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and he said: "We too heard it from Abu Hurairah." And Muslim has, through another route from Abu Hurairah, a raised report: "Allah the Exalted said: 'I bestow no blessing upon My servants except that a group of them wakes up disbelieving in it, saying: "The star, and by the star we were rained upon."'"]]

Zayd ibn Thabit recited: yunshirukum (He spreads you out). A similar usage is His saying: ﴿So disperse in the earth﴾ and ﴿Then, behold, you are human beings spreading out﴾.

If you ask: how does He make being in the ship the end point of sailing on the sea, when sailing on the sea is itself by being in the ship? I answer: He did not make being in the ship the end point of sailing on the sea. Rather, the content of the conditional clause that follows "until" (hatta), together with what it governs, is as if it were said: He makes you sail until, when this event occurs and such-and-such happens, namely the coming of a violent wind, the piling up of waves, their thinking they are about to be destroyed [[His words "and they think they are about to be destroyed" – al-Nasafi's phrasing is: "they think destruction is upon them." (Gh.)]], and the calling out for deliverance.

If you ask: what is the answer (jawab) to "idha" (when)? I answer: it is "jāathā" (it came to them). If you ask: then what of "da'aw" (they called)? I answer: it is a substitute (badal) for "zannu" (they thought), because their calling is a necessary consequence of their thinking destruction, so it is bound up with it.

If you ask: what is the benefit of turning the speech from address (the second person) to the third person (absence)? I answer: emphasis (mubalagha). It is as if He is describing their condition to others, so that they may marvel at it and so that they may be prompted to denounce and condemn it.

If you ask: what is the point of the reading of Umm al-Darda': fi al-filki, with the added ya' of nisba? I answer: it is said that both are additional letters, as in al-kharijī and al-aḥmarī. It is also permissible that it refers to the deep sea and the great water in which ships only run.

The pronoun in "jarayna" refers to the ships (al-fulk), because it is a plural of fulk, like asad, following the pattern of fu'l after fi'l, a brother of fa'l (i.e., as "fu'l" with a damma appears after "fa'l" with two fathas, like asad after asad, so the pattern "fu'l" with damma may occur in "fu'l" with damma, as fulk after fulk, because "fa'al" with two fathas and "fu'al" with damma are brothers, sharing one thing, like al-'Arab and al-'Urub, al-'Ajam and al-'Ujum, al-Rahab and al-Ruhub. Whatever is permitted in one of them is not prohibited in the other; "fu'l" with damma has been permitted in "fa'l" with fatha, so let "fu'l" with damma be permitted in "fu'l" with damma, since they are sisters. Thus in al-Sihah; consider it.) (Gh.)

In the reading of Umm al-Darda' also: "li-al-fulk," because al-fulki indicates it. "Jā'athā" means: the good wind came, i.e., met them.

It is also said: the pronoun refers to the ships. "From every place" means from all the places of the waves. "They were encompassed" means they were destroyed, the encompassing of an enemy around a people being used as a figure for destruction. "Sincere to Him in religion," without associating anything with Him, because at that time they call upon no other alongside Him. "If You deliver us," on the assumption of a saying, or because "da'awu" is part of the speech. "They act tyrannically on earth" means they corrupt in it and act wantonly, persisting in that and going to excess in it, from your saying: "The wound festered (baghā al-jurḥ) when it spread to corruption."

If you ask: what is the meaning of His words "without right" (bi-ghayr al-haqq), since tyranny cannot be with right? I answer: Yes, it can be. It is the Muslims' conquest of the lands of the unbelievers, the demolition of their houses, the burning of their crops, and the cutting of their trees, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did to the Banu Qurayza. [[Agreed upon in meaning from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both).]]

It was read: "matā' al-ḥayāt al-dunyā" (the enjoyment of the life of this world) in the accusative. If you ask: what is the difference between the two readings? I answer: when it is in the nominative, "matā'" is the predicate of the subject "baghyukum," and "'alā anfusikum" is its complement, as in His saying: ﴿So he transgressed against them﴾; the meaning is: your tyranny is only against your likes and those whose kind is your kind, i.e., some of you transgress against others for the benefit of the life of this world, which has no permanence. When it is accusative, "'alā anfusikum" is the predicate and not a complement; the meaning is: your tyranny is only a burden upon your own selves, and "matā' al-ḥayāt al-dunyā" stands in the place of an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar), as if it were said: you enjoy the enjoyment of the life of this world. It is also permissible that the nominative means: "it is the enjoyment of the life of this world," after a complete sentence.

From the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not scheme, nor help a schemer; do not transgress, nor help a transgressor; do not break faith, nor help one who breaks faith." [[Ibn al-Mubarak narrated it in al-Zuhd: Yunus ibn Yazid related to us from al-Zuhri, who said: "It has reached us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Do not scheme, nor help a schemer, for God says: ﴿And the evil scheme does not encompass except its own people﴾; do not transgress, nor help a transgressor, for God says: ﴿Your tyranny is only against your own selves﴾; do not break faith, nor help one who breaks faith, for God says: ﴿Whoever breaks faith, breaks it only to his own detriment﴾." [[Ishaq narrated it in his Musnad from Jarir from Bard ibn Yasar from Makhul, raised: "The swiftest good in reward is the maintenance of kinship ties, and the swiftest evil in punishment is tyranny and a false oath, which leave dwellings desolate." And from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him): "Were a mountain to act tyrannically against a mountain, the tyrant would be crushed." [[Al-Bukhari in al-Adab narrated: Abu Nu'aym related to us from Qatar ibn Khalifa from Abu Yahya al-Qattat, I heard Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both), as a statement of his own (mawquf). Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Anas (may God be pleased with him); Ibn Hibban cited it in al-Du'afa' in the biography of Ahmad ibn al-Fadl, and said he used to fabricate hadith.]]

Were a mountain one day to rebel against a mountain, its heights and its depths would be crushed.

This is an example of compound metaphor (al-tashbih al-murakkab): the state of this worldly life, in how swiftly it passes and how its pleasures vanish after they have come, is likened to the state of the earth's vegetation when it dries up and becomes crushed debris after it had grown thick and dense, and had adorned the earth with its greenness and lushness [[His words "wa-rafifihi," i.e., its freshness and sheen. A tree is described as "rafif" when its leaves are moistened, as stated in the Sihah. (Editor's note.)]], so that it mingled with it and became intertwined through it, until some of it intermingled with the rest. "Until, when the earth has taken its adornment and become beautified" is an eloquent expression: the earth is described as taking its adornment, by way of the image of a bride, when she takes on fine garments of every color, clothing herself and adorning herself with other kinds of finery. The original form of "izzayyanat" is "tazayyanat," which was assimilated (idgham). The reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) follows the original form. It is also read "wa-uzyinat," meaning "uf'ilat," without the verb undergoing i'lal (vowel change), like "aghyalat," meaning it became possessed of adornment. It is also read "wa-izyanat," in the pattern of "ibyada"datt. "Qadirun 'alayha" means they are able to benefit from it, to obtain its fruit, and to collect its produce. "Atahā amruna" means Our command came upon it, which is the striking of its crops with some blight after they had felt secure and certain that it had been saved. "Fa-ja'alnaha" means We made its crop "hasidan," resembling what is harvested of crops in being cut and uprooted. "Ka-an lam taghna" means as if its crop had never flourished, that is, had never grown. [[His words "ayy lam yanbut" (i.e., had not grown) is perhaps "lam yathbut" (had not remained). In the Sihah: "ghanya bil-makan" means he dwelt, and "ghanya" means he lived. (Editor's note.)]] Omitting the modified noun in these places is necessary; otherwise the meaning would not be sound. Al-Hasan read "ka-an lam yaghna" with the ya', taking the pronoun to refer to the omitted modified noun, which is the crop. It is reported from Marwan that he recited from the pulpit "ka-an lam tatghanna bil-amsi," from the verse of al-A'sha:

"Long-dwelling and long in its singing" [[The poet al-A'sha, seeking a gift from Qays ibn Ma'dikarib, says: I was a man who long remained in Iraq, long in its singing there for a long age. "Zaman" is an adverb of time; it may also be read "zamanan," like "hadhar," meaning "old." "Al-thawa'" means staying. "Ghanya bil-makan yaghna," like "radiya yardha," meant he remained and tarried, and it is said "taghanna taghannyan," like "tarahha tarhiyan," when one lingers and dwells. Thus "al-taghanni" (with doubling) is a verbal noun whose final radical is dropped at pause, though this dropping is rare. "Fa-anba'tu Qaysan" with the state that I did not come to him: despite his being far from me, that is, despite his distance, he surpassed the people of Yemen in his generosity and nobility over the people of the earth. The clause "sada" is in the position of the second object. "Al-amsu" is a metaphor for the recent time, as if it were said: "As if it had not flourished a moment ago."

Dar al-Salam (the Abode of Peace) is Paradise; He attributed it to His own Name to exalt it. It was also said that al-Salam means safety, because its people are safe from every hateful thing. And it was said: it is so called because of the abundance of greeting (salam) among them and the greeting of the angels upon them. ﴿Except the saying "Peace, peace."﴾ ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace, and guides whom He wills﴾, and those are the ones whom He knew that kindness would benefit, because His will follows His wisdom. Its meaning: He calls all the servants to the Abode of Peace, but none enter it except the guided.

**al-Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 10, verse 26:**

*al-ḥusnā* (the good reward): the good reward, *wa-ziyāda* (and an increase). What exceeds the reward is *al-tafaḍḍul* (the bounty, the extra favour). It is narrated from al-Ḥasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "ten times its like, up to seven hundredfold." ﴿And no dust [*qatar*] will cover their faces﴾: no dust will cover them, meaning a greyness with blackness in it. ﴿Nor humiliation [*dhilla*]﴾: nor any trace of disgrace and the dimness of abasement. The meaning is that what befalls the people of the Fire will not befall them, as a reminder of what Allah, by His mercy, has rescued them from. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Dust will cover it, and humiliation will cover them﴾ [Q. 80:40–41]?

If you ask: what is the connection of His saying ﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent﴾, and how does it fit with what precedes? I answer:

It is either that ﴿and those who earned﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf, coordination) with His saying ﴿those who did good﴾, as if it were said: "And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent." Or it is to be supposed: "And the recompense of those who earned evil deeds is that the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent," meaning: their recompense is that one evil deed is repaid with an evil deed like it, with nothing added to it. This second reading is more appropriate than the first, because the first involves coordination over two governing elements (ʿaṭf ʿalā ʿāmilayn), although al-Akhfash permits it. In this there is evidence that the intended meaning of the increase (al-ziyādah) is bounty (al-faḍl), for by withholding any addition to the evil deed He indicates His justice, and by affirming an addition to the reward there He indicates His bounty.

It is also read ﴿yarhaquhum dhillatun﴾ with the yāʾ (i.e., yarhaquhum, with the verb in the masculine form). ﴿Mina Allāhi min ʿāṣim﴾ means: no one can shield them from the wrath and punishment of God. It is also permissible that ﴿mā lahum min jihati Allāhi wa min ʿindihi min yaʿṣimuhum﴾ (there is for them, from the side of God and from Him, no one who protects them), just as there is for the believers. ﴿Muẓlliman﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of ﴿Allāh﴾ ... [as stated in the text: "مُظْلِماً حال من الله"]. Whoever reads ﴿qiṭaʿan﴾ with a sukūn (quiescent, unvowelled final letter), from His saying ﴿biqiṭʿin mina al-layl﴾ (with a portion of the night), makes it an attribute (ṣifah) of it, and the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb supports this:

"As if their faces were covered with pieces of the night, dark."

If you ask: when you make ﴿muẓlliman﴾ a ḥāl from ﴿al-layl﴾, what governs it? I answer: it is either that the verb ﴿ughshiyat﴾ (were covered) governs it, since ﴿min al-layl﴾ is an attribute of ﴿qiṭaʿan﴾, so its governing reaches the qualified noun just as it reaches the attribute; or that the governing element is the sense of the verb within ﴿min al-layl﴾.

Stay in your places, you and your partners. (Zamakhshari's gloss:) Keep to your places and do not move until you see what will be done to you. "And you" is a corroborating pronoun added to the pronoun in "your places," serving in place of his saying "keep to" (uzmu). "And your partners" is coordinated with it. It has been read "and your partners" with the waw taken to mean "together with," and the governing element is the sense of the verb contained in "your places." ﴿Then We separated them﴾: that is, We divided them and cut off their connections. "Al-aqran" is the plural of "qarn," with a vowel on the first letter, which is a rope with which two camels are tied together, as in al-Sihah. "Al-wasl" is the plural of "wasla," meaning connection and means, as also in al-Sihah. (Editor's note: ʿAbd al-Latif's gloss in the printed text.) Or the meaning is: We put distance between them after bringing them together at the place of standing. Their partners disowned them and their worship of them, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where are those you used to associate with God?" They will say, "They have abandoned us."﴾ It has also been read "fa-zayalna" (with an alif), like your saying "sa'ara khaddahu" and "sa'arahu," and "kallamtuhu" and "kallamtuhu." ﴿You did not used to worship us﴾: that is, you were only worshipping the devils, since they commanded you to take up rivals to God, and you obeyed them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verses 29–30:

The "in" (إِنْ) in ﴿in kunna﴾ is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafa) of the heavy "inna" (al-thaqila), and the lam is the lam that distinguishes it from the negating "in" (al-nafiya). "Them" refers to the angels, the Messiah, and whoever was worshipped besides God among those who possess reason. It has also been said: God, exalted and majestic, makes the idols speak, so they say this to them in place of the intercession they claimed and to which they attached their hopes. ﴿Hunalika﴾: in that station, in that situation, or at that time, using the name of a place for a time as a metaphor. ﴿Tabluu kullu nafsin﴾: every soul will be tested and will experience and taste what it sent forward of deeds, so it will know what they are like: whether they are ugly or good, beneficial or harmful, accepted or rejected. This is like a person who tests a thing and gets to know it in order to learn its condition. From this is God's saying: ﴿on the Day when the secrets are tested﴾ (86:9).

It is related from ʿĀṣim: "nabluu kulla nafsin" with the nun and "kulla" in the accusative, meaning: We test it by testing what it sent forward of deeds, so we know its state through knowing the state of its deeds. If the deed is good, it is happy; if it is evil, it is wretched. The meaning is: We act toward it as one who tests, like God's saying: ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾ (67:2). It is also permissible that it means: We afflict with trial, which is punishment, every sinful soul because of what it sent forward of evil. It has been read: ﴿tatlu﴾, meaning it follows what it sent forward, because its deed is what guides it to the path of Paradise or to the path of the Fire. Or it reads in its record what it has sent forward of good or evil.

﴿Mawlahumu al-haqq﴾: their Lord, the true one whose lordship is established, because they used to take as lords what has no real lordship. Or: the one who takes charge of their reckoning and reward, the just who does not wrong anyone.

It has been read: ﴿al-Haqqu﴾ with a fatha, as an emphasis on His saying ﴿they will be returned to God﴾, like your saying: "This is ʿAbd Allah, the truth, not the falsehood." Or as praise, like your saying: "Praise belongs to God, the one worthy of praise."

﴿And what they used to fabricate has strayed from them﴾: what they used to claim as partners of God was lost to them, or what they used to invent of lies and the intercession of the gods perished for them.

Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?" That is, who provides for you from both of them together. [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: who provides for you from both of them together..." etc. Ahmad said: This verse is a decisive refutation of the Qadariyya, who claim that sustenance is divided: that which God grants the servant, which is lawful, and that which the servant takes for himself, which is unlawful. This verse condemns them for this hidden shirk, if they would listen. "Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?"] He did not limit providing for you to one source, so that He might pour His bounty upon you and extend His mercy.

"Or who controls hearing and sight?" Who is able to create them and shape them to the measure of the wondrous natural form in which they were shaped. Or who protects and guards them from afflictions, despite their abundance over long periods, while they are delicate and the slightest thing harms them, by His safeguarding and preservation?

"And who manages the affair?" Who takes charge of directing the affairs of the entire world. It came with the general after the specific.

"Will you not then be wary?" Will you not guard yourselves, and fear His punishment for the error in which you are engaged?

"Then that is God, your true Lord": a reference to the One whose power and actions are these; the true One whose lordship is established beyond any doubt for whoever investigates carefully.

"So what is there after the truth but error?" That is, truth and error have no intermediary between them. Whoever transgresses the truth falls into error.

"Then how are you turned away?" From the truth to error, from monotheism to polytheism, from happiness to misery.

"Thus" (kadhalika), i.e., in the same manner: "the word of your Lord has come true" (haqqat kalimatu rabbika), i.e., just as it is established and confirmed that after the truth there is only error, or just as it is established that they are turned away from the truth, so likewise the word of your Lord has come true "against those who defied" (ʿala alladhina fasaqu), i.e., rebelled in their disbelief and went to its furthest extreme. "That they do not believe" (annahum la yu'minun) is a substitution for "the word" (al-kalima): i.e., it is established against them that faith is negated, and God knew this about them. Or: the word of God has come true against them, that they are among the forsaken, and that their faith will not occur. Or he intended by "the word": the promise of punishment, and "that they do not believe" is a causal clause, meaning: because they do not believe.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 34–35:

If you say: how is it said to them, ﴿Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ when they do not acknowledge the repetition (of creation)? I say: the repetition of creation has been placed where its proof is manifest, in the position of what, if anyone raised it, would be a stubborn denier, rejecting an evident truth in which no doubt can enter. This indicates that in denying it they deny something accepted and acknowledged as sound by rational people. And He said to His Prophet ﷺ, ﴿Say: Allah originates creation and then repeats it﴾, commanding him to speak on their behalf in the reply. That is, He does not leave them, in their obstinacy and stubbornness, to utter the word of truth, so He speaks on their behalf. It is said: "he guided him to the truth" and "to the truth," combining both constructions. It is also said: "hada" (he guided) used intransitively with the meaning of "ihtada" (he was guided), just as "shara" is used with the meaning of "ishtara" (he bought). From this is His saying, ﴿Or is one who does not guide [unless he is guided]?﴾ [[The phrase "Or is one who does not guide" is from their saying "hada bi-nafsihi" (he guided himself): "am man la yahiddi" (or the one who does not guide), like "yarmi" (he throws). As for "bi-fath al-ha'" (with a fatha on the ha') ... etc.: the reading with its kasra together with the shadda remains, and he indicated it with his words "or it was kasra'd." The reading "yarmi" belongs to Hamza and Ali. With fatha and shadda it is for al-Makki and al-Shami. With kasra and shadda it is for 'Asim. The original is "yahtadi" (he is guided), and this is the reading of 'Abd Allah, as reported by al-Nasafi. (ʿAyn)]] It is also read as ﴿la yuhaddi﴾ with a fatha and with a kasra on the ha', with the dal doubled. The original is "yahtadi," which was assimilated, and the ha' took a fatha by the movement of the ta', or was given a kasra to resolve the meeting of two sakins, and the ya' was given a kasra to follow what comes after it. It is also read: ﴿illa an yuhda﴾ from "hadahu" and "haddahu" for intensification. From this is their saying "tahadda" (he is guided). Its meaning is that Allah alone is the One who guides to the truth, by means of the intellects He placed in those who are obligated and the capacity He gave them to reflect upon the proofs He set up for them, and by means of His kindness toward them, His granting them success, His inspiring them, His bringing things to their minds, and His making them stand upon the laws. So, is there any of your partners whom you have made equals to Allah, from among the most noble of them, such as the angels, the Messiah, and 'Uzayr, who guides to the truth with a guidance like the guidance of Allah? Then He said: ﴿Is then one who guides to the truth with this guidance more worthy to be followed, or one who does not guide, i.e., does not guide himself, or does not guide others unless he is guided by Allah?﴾ It is said: its meaning is: or one of the idols who does not find his way to a place so as to move to it, ﴿unless he is carried﴾, i.e., unless he is moved; or one who is not guided, and it is not valid for him to be guided unless Allah moves him from his state until He makes him an animal obligated (to act) and then guides him. ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge﴾ falsely, in that you claim that they are equals to Allah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 45:

"As though they had not tarried but an hour of the day." They estimate the time of their staying in the world. It is also said: in the graves, owing to the terror of what they see.

"Recognizing one another": each one recognizes the other, as though they had not parted but a little while. This occurs at their coming out of the graves; then the recognition among them ceases because of the severity of the matter upon them.

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of "as though they had not tarried" and "recognizing one another"? I say: as for the first, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to "them", meaning: He gathers them while they are as those who did not tarry but an hour. As for the second, it may either be linked to the adverbial expression (ẓarf) or it may be explanatory (mubayyinah) of His saying "as though they had not tarried but an hour", because recognition does not persist over a long lapse of time, and it turns into mutual denial.

"They have certainly lost" is said with the implied sense of "saying": that is, they recognize one another among themselves, saying that; or it is a testimony from God Most High to their loss. The meaning is that they have squandered in their trade [[Note: his words "squandered in their trade": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "al-rajul wa'awḍa' fī tijāratihi" (with the verb in the passive form, unnamed agent) means "wa ḍa'an fīhimā," i.e., he lost. (ʿ)]] and in their exchange of faith for disbelief, "and they were not guided" in the trade, not knowing it. This is a resumptive clause carrying the sense of wonder, as though it were said: how great is their loss!

Then to Us is their return. The answer to "nutawaffiyanaka" (We cause you to die) is "fa-ilayna marji'uhum," and the answer to "nurinnaka" (We show you) is omitted. It is as if it were said: "And whether We show you some of what We threaten them with in this world, so be it; or We cause you to die before We show it to you, and We will show it to you in the Hereafter." Then, if you say: God is a witness over what they do in both abodes (al-darayn), so what is the meaning of "thumma" (then)? I say: The witnessing was mentioned while what is intended is its consequence and result, which is the punishment. It is as if He said: "Then God is one who punishes them for what they do." Ibn Abi Ablah read "thumma" with a fatha, meaning "there" (hunalika). It is also permissible that what is meant is: God executes His testimony regarding their deeds on the Day of Resurrection, when their skins, tongues, hands and feet speak out as witnesses against them.

For every nation there is a messenger. He is sent to them to awaken them to monotheism (tawhid) and to call them to the religion of truth. ﴿So when their messenger comes to them with clear proofs, and they deny him and do not follow him, judgment is passed between them﴾, that is, between the Prophet and those who denied him, ﴿with justice﴾, meaning with fairness. So the messenger is delivered and the deniers are punished. This is like His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We had sent a messenger﴾.

Or, it means: for every nation among the nations, on the Day of Resurrection there is a messenger to whom they are attributed and by whom they are called. So when their messenger comes to the place of standing (al-Mawqif) to bear witness against them concerning disbelief and belief, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the prophets and the witnesses will be brought, and judgment will be passed between them with truth﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 48–49:

"When will this promise be fulfilled?" It is a demand for hastening the punishment they were promised, deeming it far-fetched. ﴿I have no power over myself to harm or benefit,﴾ harm such as sickness or poverty, and benefit such as health or wealth, ﴿except what Allah wills.﴾ This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'): that is, "but what Allah wills of that is certain to occur. So how could I have power to bring harm upon you or to bring the punishment?" ﴿For every nation there is a term.﴾ This means that your punishment has a term appointed by Allah, a limit fixed in time. ﴿When their term comes, they will not be able to delay it by an hour, nor advance it,﴾ and when that time arrives He will certainly fulfil His promise to you, so do not seek to hasten it. Ibn Sirin recited: "fa-idha jaa' ajaluhum" (when their terms come).

The adverbial accusative *bayatan* (بَياتاً) is in the accusative of time (*zarf*, an adverb of time), meaning "at a time of nighttime attack." If you ask, "Why not say *layan* (at night) or *nahāran* (by day)?" the answer is:

It is intended to mean: "If His punishment comes upon you at a time of *bayāt* (a night raid), it will fall upon you while you are heedless, asleep, unaware, just as an enemy launches a surprise attack at night." *Bayāt* is used here in the sense of *tabyīt* (a night attack), just as *salām* is used in the sense of *taslīm* (greeting). Likewise, *nahāran* (نَهاراً) means "at a time when you are occupied with seeking your livelihood and earnings." Similar is the verse ﴿Are they secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?﴾ (7:97), and ﴿or in the forenoon while they are at play?﴾ (7:98).

The pronoun in *minhu* (مِنْهُ) refers to the punishment. The meaning is: all punishment is hateful, bitter in taste, and causes aversion, so what is there about it that they should seek to hasten, when nothing in it calls for hastening?

It is also permissible that the meaning be one of astonishment, as if it were said: "What terrible, severe calamity they seek to hasten!" In this case, *min* (مِنْ) must be explanatory (*lil-bayān*). It has also been said that the pronoun in *minhu* refers to God Most High.

If you ask: To what does the interrogative *mādhā* (ماذا) relate, and where is the answer to the conditional? The answer: it relates to *araytum* (أَرَأَيْتُمْ), because the meaning is: "Tell me, what is it that the criminals seek to hasten?" The answer to the conditional is omitted, and it is: "you would regret hastening it, or you would recognize the error in it."

If you ask: Why was it not said, "What do you seek to hasten of it?" The author Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "If you ask, why was it not said, 'What do you seek to hasten of it?'…" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: In this eloquent expression there are two subtleties: the first is the placing of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun; the second is the mention of the apparent noun in an additional form suited to the verbal noun (*maṣdar*). Each of them stands independently as a aspect of rhetoric and emphasis, and God knows best.

[The answer is:] the intention is to indicate the reason for abandoning hastening, which is criminality, because it is incumbent upon the criminal to fear punishment for his crime and to be terrified of its coming, even if it is delayed, let alone to seek to hasten it.

It is also permissible that *mādhā yastaʿjilu minhu al-mujrimūn* (مَاذا يَسْتَعْجِلُ مِنْهُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ) be the answer to the condition, like your saying: "If I come to you, what will you feed me?" Then the clause relates to *araytum*. And it is permissible that *athumma idhā mā waqaʿa āmantum bihi* (أَثُمَّ إِذا ما وَقَعَ آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ) be the answer to the condition, with *mādhā yastaʿjilu minhu al-mujrimūn* being a parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ*). The meaning is: "If His punishment comes upon you, will you believe in it after it has occurred, when faith will no longer benefit you?" The entry of the interrogative particle upon *thumma* is like its entry upon the *wāw* and *fā'* in ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure…﴾ (7:97–98).

*Ālān* (آلْآنَ) is according to the supposition of a saying (*ʿalā irādat al-qawl*), meaning: It will be said to them when they believe after the punishment has occurred: ﴿Now? And you used to hasten it!﴾ (10:51) — i.e., "and you used to deny it," because their hastening was in the manner of denial and rejection.

It is also read *ālān* (آلان), with the omission of the hamza that follows the *lām*, and its vowel is placed upon the *lām*. ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong﴾ (10:52) is conjoined to the implied *qīla* (it was said) before *ālān*.

Wa-yastanbi'unaka (wa-yastakhbirunaka), fa-yaqulun: a-haqqun huwa? This is a question in the mode of denial and mockery.

Al-A'mash recited: ālḥaqqu huwa, and this is more emphatic in mockery, since it implies the sense of insinuation that it is false. That is because the alif-lam is for the genus, so it is as if it were said: Is it the truth and not falsehood? Or is it that which you named "the truth"? The pronoun refers to the promised punishment.

Iy (إِي) is in the sense of "yes" only in oaths, just as hal (هل) is in the sense of qad (قد) only in questions. I have heard them say in affirmation: iywa, joining it to the oath particle waw and not pronouncing it alone.

Wa-ma antum bi-mu'jizin: you will not escape (bi-fa'itin) the punishment, and it will certainly overtake them without doubt.

"ظَلَمَتْ" is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "nafs" (soul), meaning "every wrongdoing soul." Here it says: "And if every wrongdoing soul possessed whatever is on the earth, i.e., in the world today, of its treasures, wealth and all its benefits, despite their abundance, it would ransom itself with it, that is, would make it a ransom for itself." It is said: "fada-hu fa-ftada" (he ransomed him, so he ransomed himself), and it is also said: "iftada-hu," which has the same meaning as "fada-hu."

"وَأَسَرُّوا النَّدامَةَ لَمَّا رَأَوُا الْعَذابَ" means: because they were stunned at seeing what they had not expected and had not imagined, and they witnessed such severity and magnitude of the matter that it stripped them of their strength and overwhelmed them. So they could not endure any weeping, shouting, or what the distressed person does, except concealing regret and anguish within their hearts. This is like the condemned man being led to the gallows, whom the violence of the calamity that has struck him overwhelms, until he is so overcome that he cannot utter a word (قوله «لا ينبس بكلمة» أى لا يتكلم. أفاده الصحاح. (ع)) and remains rigid and bewildered.

It is also said: their leaders concealed their regret from their lowly followers whom they had misled, out of shame before them and fear of their reproach. It is also said: "asarruha" means "they made it pure," either because concealing it is its sincerity, or from the saying "sirr al-shay'," meaning the purest part of a thing. In this there is mockery of them and of their errors at the time of sincere regret.

It is also said: "asarru al-nadamah" means "they displayed it," from the saying "asarra al-shay'" and "ashara-hu," meaning he made it apparent. There is no endurance there.

"وَقُضِيَ بَيْنَهُمْ" means: between the wrongdoers and the wronged, as indicated by the mention of wrongdoing.

Then he follows this with the declaration that to Him belongs all sovereignty, that He is the One who rewards and punishes, that what He has promised of reward and punishment is true, that He is the One able to give life and cause death, and that none other can do so, and that the return is to His reckoning and recompense, so that it may be known that the matter is so, and one fears and hopes, and those who are deceived are not deluded by it.

﴿Indeed, there has come to you an admonition﴾: that is, there has come to you a book that combines these benefits: an admonition and a reminder of monotheism (tawhid). ﴿And it is a healing﴾: that is, a remedy for what is in your breasts of corrupt beliefs, and a call to the truth. ﴿And a mercy﴾ for whoever among you believes in it.

The original sense is: "By the bounty of God and His mercy, let them rejoice." So: "By that, let them rejoice."

The repetition serves emphasis and confirmation, and it makes the bounty and mercy the exclusive objects of rejoicing, to the exclusion of whatever else the worldly life offers. One of the two verbs has been omitted because the mentioned one indicates it. The fa' (so) carries the meaning of a condition, as if it were said: "If they rejoice in anything, let them single out these two for rejoicing, for there is nothing more deserving of joy than these two."

It may also be understood as: "By the bounty of God and His mercy, let them strive; so by that, let them rejoice." It may also be understood as: "There has come to you an admonition through the bounty of God and His mercy; so by its coming, let them rejoice."

It was also recited as ﴿فَلْتَفْرَحُوا﴾ with the ta' (تاء), and this is the original and the regular form. It is reported to be the recitation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also transmitted from him [[This is a fragment of a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi from the narration of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was late for us in the dawn prayer, until the sun almost rose. Then he came out, the prayer was called, and he led us in a prayer that was brief. When he finished the salam, he said: 'Are you not in your rows?' — the hadith."]] the words "﴿لِتَأْخُذُوا مَضَاجِعَكُمْ﴾" (so that you may take your resting places), which he said on some campaigns.

In the recitation of Ubayy, it is ﴿فَافْرَحُوا﴾ (so rejoice). The pronoun in ﴿هُوَ﴾ refers back to that. It was also recited ﴿مِمَّا تَجْمَعُونَ﴾ with the ya' and with the ta' (i.e., "what they gather" read as "you gather").

It is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) recited ﴿قُلْ بِفَضْلِ اللَّهِ وَبِرَحْمَتِهِ﴾ and said: "By the Book of God and Islam" [[Ibn Abi Shaybah recorded it through Mujahid from Ibn Abbas regarding God's words ﴿قُلْ بِفَضْلِ اللَّهِ﴾ and mentioned it. Similarly, al-Tabari recorded it from Abu Sa'id. It is also said that His bounty is Islam, and His mercy is what He promised for it.

﴿Indeed, there has come to you an admonition﴾: that is, there has come to you a book that combines these benefits: an admonition and a reminder of monotheism (tawhid). ﴿And it is a healing﴾: that is, a remedy for what is in your breasts of corrupt beliefs, and a call to the truth. ﴿And a mercy﴾ for whoever among you believes in it.

The original sense is: "By the bounty of God and His mercy, let them rejoice." So: "By that, let them rejoice."

The repetition serves emphasis and confirmation, and it makes the bounty and mercy the exclusive objects of rejoicing, to the exclusion of whatever else the worldly life offers. One of the two verbs has been omitted because the mentioned one indicates it. The fa' (so) carries the meaning of a condition, as if it were said: "If they rejoice in anything, let them single out these two for rejoicing, for there is nothing more deserving of joy than these two."

It may also be understood as: "By the bounty of God and His mercy, let them strive; so by that, let them rejoice." It may also be understood as: "There has come to you an admonition through the bounty of God and His mercy; so by its coming, let them rejoice."

It was also recited as ﴿فَلْتَفْرَحُوا﴾ with the ta' (تاء), and this is the original and the regular form. It is reported to be the recitation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 59–60:

﴿Tell me﴾ (أَرَأَيْتُمْ): أخبرونى. And ﴿what God has sent down﴾ (وما أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ): "ما" is in the accusative position, governed by "anzala" (sent down), or by "ara'aytum" (tell me), with the meaning: "inform me of it." ﴿Then you made of it unlawful and lawful﴾ (فَجَعَلْتُمْ مِنْهُ حَراماً وَحَلالًا): that is, God sent it down as entirely lawful provision, and you divided it up and said, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," like their saying, ﴿These are cattle and tilth, forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we wish, by their claim; and these are cattle whose backs are forbidden, and cattle over which the name of God is not mentioned, inventing falsehood against Him﴾ (هذِهِ أَنْعامٌ وَحَرْثٌ حِجْرٌ، ما فِي بُطُونِ هذِهِ الْأَنْعامِ خالِصَةٌ لِذُكُورِنا وَمُحَرَّمٌ عَلى أَزْواجِنا): "What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives." ﴿Did God permit you?﴾ (آللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمْ): this is connected to "ara'aytum." ﴿Say﴾ (وقل): this is repeated for emphasis.

The meaning is: "Inform me, did God permit you to make things lawful and unlawful, so that you do this by His permission, or do you fabricate lies against God in attributing that to Him?" It is also permissible for the hamza to be interrogative of denial, and "am" to be disjunctive, meaning "rather": ﴿Or do you fabricate against God?﴾ (أم تتكذبون... أتفترون على الله), establishing the fabrication. This verse is sufficient as a powerful restraint against recklessness regarding the rulings that are asked about, and it urges caution in them, so that no one says of anything, permissible or impermissible, except after certainty and precision. Whoever is not certain should fear God and remain silent; otherwise he is a fabricator against God.

﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ (يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ): this is governed by "al-zann" (assumption), and it is an assumption that actually occurs in it. That is: what will the fabricators assume on that day about what will be done to them, the day of recompense for good and evil? This is a great threat, since its matter is left vague. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read ﴿And what do they assume﴾ (وما ظنّ), in the verbal form, meaning: "What assumption will they have assumed on the Day of Resurrection?" It was stated in the past tense because it is certain to happen, so it is as though it has already occurred.

﴿Indeed, God is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ (إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَذُو فَضْلٍ عَلَى النَّاسِ): in that He has bestowed upon them reason, showed them mercy through revelation, and taught them the lawful and the unlawful. ﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾ (وَلكِنَّ أَكْثَرَهُمْ لا يَشْكُرُونَ): for this blessing, and they do not follow what they have been guided to.

The pronoun in minhu refers to the shaʾn, because reciting the Qur'an is one of the matters of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), indeed the greatest of his matters. Or it refers to the revelation (al-tanzil), as if it were said: "and you do not recite from the revelation any Qur'an," since every part of it is Qur'an. The pronoun placed before its mention is an expression of its magnificence. Or it refers to God, Mighty and Majestic.

"And you do not do any deed, and you (all) do not do any deed" (wa-mā taʿmalūna antum jamīʿan min ʿamal), of whatever kind it may be, "but We are witnesses over you" (illā kunnā ʿalaykum shuhūdan), meaning watchers (shāhidīn), guardians (ruqabāʾ), "We take account of you" (nuhsī ʿalaykum), "when you are immersed in it" (idh tufīḍūna fīh). One says "afāḍa fī al-amr" when he rushes into the matter.

"And there is not hidden" (wa-mā yaʿzubu), it is read with a damma and with a kasra: meaning "does not go far" and "is not concealed." From this comes "al-rawḍ al-ʿāzib" (the distant meadow).

"Nor is there anything smaller than that, nor larger" (wa-lā aṣghara min dhālika wa-lā akbar). The reading is with the accusative and with the nominative. The preferred reading is the accusative, by negating the genus (nafy al-jins). The nominative is by beginning a new sentence, so that it stands as an independent statement. Regarding conjoining it to the place of "min mithqāli dharratin" (its locative position) or to the form of "mithqāli dharratin," with the fatḥa in the genitive position because of the prohibition of declension (imtināʿ al-ṣarf), there is a difficulty, because your saying "nothing is hidden from Him except that it is in a Book" is problematic.

If you ask: why did you place the earth before the heavens, contrary to His saying in Surat Saba, "Knower of the unseen; not an atom's weight is hidden from Him in the heavens or in the earth" (ʿĀlimi al-ghayb, lā yaʿzubu ʿanhu mithqālu dharratin fī al-samāwāti wa-lā fī al-arḍ)? I say:

The heavens deserve to be placed before the earth. But when He mentioned His witnessing over the affairs of the people of the earth, their conditions and their deeds, and connected to that His saying "not hidden from Him," it was appropriate to place the earth before the heavens. Moreover, the conjunction with "wa" (and) carries the same ruling as the dual.

The awliya' of God (awliya', "friends" or "allies") are those who take Him as their ally through obedience, and He takes them as His allies through honour. He explained this in His saying: ﴿those who believe and are mindful of God﴾. So their taking Him as ally is ﴿for them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾, which is His taking them as allies.

It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked: "Who are the awliya' of God?"

He said: "They are those whom seeing causes God to be remembered," meaning their bearing and comportment.[[Ibn Abi Shaybah reported it through Ash'ath ibn Ishaq from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah from him, and Ibn Mardawayh through Yahya al-Hammami from Ya'qub al-Sahmi from Ja'far likewise. Al-Nasa'i and al-Bazzar connected it through Muhammad ibn Sa'id ibn Sabiq from Ya'qub, mentioning Ibn 'Abbas: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the awliya' of God, and he said: 'Those who, when they are seen, God is remembered.' Al-Bazzar said: Someone other than Muhammad narrated it from Ya'qub without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas."]]

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him): they are those marked by humility and tranquillity.

It has been said: they are those who love one another for God's sake.

It is narrated from 'Umar (may God be pleased with him): "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'Among God's servants are those who are neither prophets nor martyrs, yet the prophets and martyrs will envy them on the Day of Resurrection because of their station with God.'" They said: "O Messenger of God, tell us who they are and what their deeds are, so that we may love them." He said: "They are a people who love one another for God's sake, with no family ties between them and no wealth they exchange. By God, their faces are light, and they are upon pulpits of light. Then he recited the verse.[[Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, al-Tabari, Abu Nu'aym in the opening of al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab reported it through Jarir from 'Umarah ibn Ghaziyyah from Abu Zur'ah from 'Umar. And let not their speech grieve you. [Read as] "wa-la yuhzinka" (from ahzanahu): their speech, their denial of you, their threats, their consultation about plotting your destruction and nullifying your affair, and all else they say concerning you. ﴿Indeed, all might (al-'izzah) belongs to Allah﴾ is a resumption (isti'naf) carrying the sense of causal explanation (ta'lil), as if it were said: "Why should I not grieve?" So it is said: "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah," meaning that dominance and subjugation are wholly in the dominion of Allah; none possesses any part of them, neither they nor others. So He overcomes them and gives you victory over them. ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers shall surely prevail." Indeed, We shall help Our messengers﴾.

Abu Haywah read: "anna al-'izzata" with a fatha, meaning "because might belongs to Allah," which is an explicit causal particle. As for one who takes it as a substitute (badal) for "qawluhum" and then rejects it, the rejected thing is his parsing of it, not the reading itself that he rejected.

﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: He hears what they say and knows what they plot and resolve upon. And He will requite them for that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 66:

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ — that is, the rational beings who discern (al-'uqala' al-mumayyizun), namely the angels and the two species (al-thaqalan, humankind and jinn). He specified them to indicate that these, when they belong to Him and are under His dominion, are all servants, while He, glorified and exalted is He, is their Lord, and none of them is fit for lordship (al-rububiyya) or to be a partner to Him in it. Therefore, whatever is beyond them, of things that do not reason, is more deserving of not being a rival (nidd) and partner to Him. It also shows that whoever takes other than Him as a lord, whether a king or a human, let alone an idol or something else, is a falsifier who follows what blind imitation (taqlid) and abandonment of reflection (tark al-nazar) have led him to.

As for the meaning of ﴿And they do not follow partners﴾: that is, they do not truly follow the partners, even though they call them partners, because the partnership of God in lordship is impossible. ﴿They follow only their own assumption that they are partners, and they merely guess﴾ (yakhrusun): they estimate and conjecture that they are partners, a baseless estimation.

It is permissible for ﴿wa-ma yattabi'u﴾ to carry the sense of interrogation, meaning: "And what do they follow?" In that case, "partners" (shuraka') is in the accusative governed by "yad'un" (they call upon), and in the first reading it is governed by "yattabi'u." The original construction would have been: "And what do those who call upon other than God as partners follow? Partners," but he limited it to one of the two for the sake of indication.

It is also permissible for "ma" to be a relative pronoun conjoined to "man" (whoever), as if it were said: "To God belongs what those who call upon other than God as partners follow," that is, "and to Him belong their partners."

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) read "tad'un" with the ta' (second person). Its justification is to take ﴿wa-ma yattabi'u﴾ as an interrogative, meaning: "And what do those whom you call partners—from among the angels and prophets—follow?" That is, they follow God and obey Him, so why do you not do the like of their deeds? This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord﴾. Then he turned the speech from address (khitab) to the third person (ghayba), saying: ﴿The polytheists follow only conjecture, and they do not follow what the angels and prophets follow of the truth.﴾

Then He drew attention to His great power and His all-encompassing blessing upon His servants, by which He deserves to be worshipped as one God alone: He made the night dark for them so that they might find rest in it from the exhaustion they suffer during the day from the toil of going back and forth in pursuit of livelihood, and made the day bright so that they might see in it the means of their sustenance and their gains. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen﴾, listening with reflection and taking heed.

Glory be to Him: a declaration of His transcendence above having a son, and an expression of wonder at their foolish saying.

He is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani): this is the reason for negating a son, because what a son is sought for is one who begets, and what begetting is sought for is need in every case. So whoever is free of need, a son is negated from him.

To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth: so He is self-sufficient by His dominion over them, and has no need to take any of them as a son.

"You have no authority for this." That is, you have no proof for this saying. The preposition "bi" (with/for) properly should be attached to the verb in "inda-kum" (you have), so that the saying takes the place of the authority, as when you say: "What you have in your land is bananas (ma 'indakum bi-ardikum mawz)," as if it were said: "You have, in what you say, an authority."

"Do you say about Allah what you do not know?" Since He negated proof from them, He made them ignorant. This indicates that every saying for which the speaker has no proof is ignorance, and is not knowledge.

Those who invent lies against Allah by ascribing a son to Him. "A brief enjoyment in this world": that is, their fabricating this is a small benefit in the worldly life, since through it they maintain their leadership in disbelief and their opposition to the Prophet (ﷺ) by openly displaying it. Then after that they will meet with everlasting misery.

﴿كَبُرَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: عَظُمَ عليكم، وشَقَّ وثَقُلَ. ومنها قوله تعالى: ﴿وَإِنَّها لَكَبِيرَةٌ إِلَّا عَلَى الْخاشِعِينَ﴾. ويقال: تعاظمه الأمر. ﴿مَقامِي﴾: مكاني، يعني نفسه، كما تقول: فعلتُ كذا لمكان فلان. وفلان ثقيل الظل. ومنه ﴿وَلِمَنْ خافَ مَقامَ رَبِّهِ﴾ بمعنى: خاف ربه. أو: ﴿قِيامِي﴾ [[قوله «أو قيامي ومكثي» لعله أو مقامي بالضم. (ع)]] و﴿مَكْثِي بَيْنَ أَظْهُرِكُمْ مُدَداً طِوالاً أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ إِلَّا خَمْسِينَ عاماً﴾. أو: ﴿مَقامِي﴾ [[قوله «أو مقامي وتذكيري» لعل هذا أو قيامي. (ع)]] و﴿تَذْكِيرِي﴾، لأنهم كانوا إذا وعظوا الجماعة قاموا على أرجلهم يعظونهم، ليكون مكانهم بيِّناً وكلامهم مسموعاً، كما يُحكى عن عيسى صلوات الله عليه أنه كان يعظ الحواريين قائماً وهم قعود.

﴿فَأَجْمِعُوا أَمْرَكُمْ وَشُرَكاءَكُمْ﴾: من أجمع الأمرَ وأزمعه، إذا نواه وعزم عليه. قال:

هَلْ أَغْدُوَنْ يَوْماً وَأَمْرِي مُجْمَعُ [[يا ليت شعري والحوادث جمة ... هل أغدون يوما وأمرى مجمع

قوله «والحوادث جمة» أي كثيرة. جملة اعتراضية. وأغدون: مؤكد بالنون الخفيفة. وأمري مجمع: أي منوي مجزوم بامتثاله. أو المعنى: وشملي مجتمع بعد تفرقه، وهي جملة حالية مغنية عن خبر أغدون. أو خبرها. وزيدت الواو لتوكيد الربط. وأجمع يتعلق بالمعقول، وجمع يتعلق بالمحسوس.]]

والواو بمعنى «مع»، يعني: فأجمعوا أمركم مع شركائكم. وقرأ الحسن: ﴿وَشُرَكاؤُكُمْ﴾ بالرفع، عطفاً على الضمير المتصل، وجاز من غير توكيد بالمنفصل لقيام الفاصل مقامه لطول الكلام، كما تقول: اضرب زيداً وعمرو. وقُرئ: ﴿فَاجْمَعُوا﴾ من الجمع. و﴿شُرَكاءَكُمْ﴾ نصب للعطف على المفعول، أو لأنّ الواو بمعنى «مع». وفي قراءة أُبيّ: ﴿فَأَجْمِعُوا أَمْرَكُمْ وَادْعُوا شُرَكاءَكُمْ﴾.

فإن قلت: كيف جاز إسناد الإجماع إلى الشركاء؟ قلت: على وجه التهكم، كقوله ﴿قُلِ ادْعُوا شُرَكاءَكُمْ ثُمَّ كِيدُونِ﴾.

فإن قلت: ما معنى الأمرين؟ أمرُهم الذي يجمعونه، وأمرُهم الذي لا يكون عليهم غُمّة؟ قلت: أمّا الأمر الأول فالقصد إلى إهلاكه، يعني: فأجمعوا ما تريدون من إهلاكي، واحتشدوا فيه، وابذلوا وسعكم في كيدي. وإنما قال ذلك إظهاراً لقلة مبالاته، وثقته بما وعده ربه من كلاءته وعصمته إياه، وأنهم لن يجدوا إليه سبيلاً. وأما الثاني ففيه وجهان، أحدهما: أن يراد مصاحبتهم له وما كانوا فيه معه من الحال الشديدة عليهم المكروهة عندهم، يعني: ثم أهلكوني لئلا يكون عيشكم بسببي غُصّة وحالكم عليكم غُمّة: أي غماً وهماً. والغَمّ والغُمّة، كالكَرْب والكُرْبة. والثاني أن يراد به ما أُريد بالأمر الأول، والغُمّة السترة من غَمَّه إذا ستره.

ومنها قوله ﷺ: «ولا غُمّة في فرائض الله» [[هو طرف من حديث وائل بن حجر في كتاب النبي ﷺ إلى الأقيال، وفيه: «ولا يوصم في الدين ولا غمة في فرائض الله» وقال: الغمة السترة، أي لا تستر في فرائض الله، بل ظاهر بها.]] أي لا تُستر، ولكن يُجاهَر بها، يعني: ولا يكن قصدكم إلى إهلاكي مستوراً [[قوله «مستورا عليكم» لعله أراد ملتبسا، فلذا قال عليكم، كما أشار إليه النسفي. (ع)]] عليكم، ولكن مكشوفاً مشهوراً تجاهرونني به.
