Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 74:

﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples﴾, meaning: after Noah, [We sent] Hud, Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb. ﴿So they came to them with clear proofs﴾, that is, with evident arguments establishing their claim. ﴿But they were not going to believe﴾, meaning: their faith was as impossible as something unattainable, because of the severity of their obstinacy in disbelief and their determination upon it. ﴿Because of what they had denied before﴾, he means that before the sending of the messengers they were people of ignorance (jahiliyya) who denied the truth. So there was no difference between their state after the sending of the messengers and their state before it, as though no one had been sent to them. ﴿Thus do We seal﴾, that is, with a seal of the same firm kind, ﴿upon the hearts of the transgressors﴾. The sealing functions as a metaphor (kinaya) for their obstinacy and persistence in stubbornness, because abandonment (khidhlan) follows from it. Do you not see how He attributed transgression (i'tida') to them and described them with it?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on surah 10, verses 75–78:

"After them" means after the messengers. "With Our signs" means with the nine signs. "﴿They were arrogant﴾" means they were arrogant about accepting them. The greatest arrogance is for servants to treat lightly the message of their Lord after it has been made clear, and to make themselves great by refusing to accept it. "﴿And they were a people of criminals﴾" means disbelievers, possessors of great sins. Therefore they were arrogant toward it and dared to reject it. "﴿When the truth came to them from Us﴾" means when they recognized that it is the truth and that it comes from God, not from Moses and Aaron. "﴿They said﴾," because of their love of desires, "﴿This is clearly sorcery﴾." And they knew that the truth is further from sorcery than anything, since sorcery is nothing but deception and falsehood.

If you say: they asserted by their saying "This is clearly sorcery" that it is sorcery, [[Mahmud said: "If you say: they asserted by their saying 'This is clearly sorcery' that it is sorcery... etc." Ahmad said: There is some obscurity in the difference between the two aspects. Its clarification is that the saying in the first aspect occurs as a metonymy (kināya) for defect, so it does not require an object (maf'ūl). In the second, it is taken as requiring an object. And God knows best.]] then how was it said to them, "﴿Do you say it is sorcery?﴾"

I answer: there are several aspects.

The first: the meaning of His saying "﴿Do you say of the truth...﴾" is: do you find fault with it and disparage it? You should have submitted to it and magnified it. This is from the saying "﴿he does not fear the calumny﴾" (al-qāla), and among people there is taqāwul when one says to another what offends him. The word "al-qawl" here has the sense of "al-dhikr," as in His saying: "﴿We heard a youth mention them﴾" (yadhkuruhum). Then He said "﴿Is this sorcery?﴾", denying what they said in finding fault with it and disparaging it.

The second: the object of "﴿Do you say﴾" is omitted, and it is what is indicated by their saying "﴿This is clearly sorcery﴾", as if it were said: "Do you say what you say?", meaning their saying "This is clearly sorcery." Then it was said: "Is this sorcery?"

The third: the clause "﴿Is this sorcery? The sorcerers do not prosper﴾" is a quotation of their speech, as if they had said: "Have you come with sorcery, seeking success by it?" And "﴿the sorcerers do not prosper﴾" is like Moses saying to the sorcerers: "﴿What you have brought is sorcery; surely God will nullify it﴾."

"﴿To turn us away﴾" means to divert us. Lafta and fatla are two cognate verbs, and their intransitive forms are iltifāt and infitāl. "﴿From what we found our fathers upon﴾" means the worship of idols. "﴿And that greatness (al-kibriyā') be yours both﴾" means dominion (al-mulk), because kings are described as proud (mutakabbirūn). For this reason the king is called "al-jabbār" (the compeller), and he is described with "al-saydu" and "al-shūs" (haughty and arrogant). For this reason Ibn al-Ruqayyat described Mus'ab in his saying:

*"His rule is the rule of mercy, in which there is no tyranny (jabarūt) from him, nor pride (kibriyā')."*

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 10, verse 88:**

So he invoked God against them with what he knew could not be other than it, just as you say: "May God curse Iblis," or "May God disgrace the disbelievers," while you know that it cannot be otherwise. [[His words "yatasakkaʿūn": in the *Sihah*, *al-taskuʿ* is persistence in falsehood. (ʿ)]] It is as if he said: "Let them persist in the misguidance they are upon."

And that they may become misguided [[His words "and that they may become misguided": this is according to the reading *liyaḍillū* with an open *yāʾ* (i.e., *liyaḍillū* read with fatḥa on the yāʾ). (ʿ)]] and that God may seal their hearts so that they do not believe; and I am not concerned about them, they are most deserving of that and more. [[His words "and out of anger toward him": in the *Sihah*, *al-ḥard* (with a vowel on the first letter) is anger. (ʿ)]]

He likened the covenants of safe-conduct that one takes from a tribe, by which one secures oneself and reaches another, to cords, in a metaphor of the explicit kind. That is: when we undertake to pass beyond the covenants of a tribe and bear the hardship of crossing the place of their protection, then the attribution of crossing to the cords is a rational metaphor (majāz 'aqlī). My she-camel took cords from the other tribe while going to you, that is covenants to reach the other tribe, and so on. Attributing the taking to the camel is also a rational metaphor, and its connection is sufficed by her proximity to it at the time of the action. He attributed it to her for emphasis and to imagine that she knows the praised one and his merit, so she travels to him herself. It is also narrated as "yujawwizuhā." And "jibāl" with a jīm: then the meaning of "akhadhat" is: she cut across the land of the other tribe, traveling to you, mountains other than those. In any case, this indicates the difficulty of the road.

It is not from this, because if it were, the correct form would be "wa-jawwaznā banī Isrā'īl fī al-baḥr," as in the verse:

"Wa-lā budda min jārin yujīzu sabīlahā / kamā jawwaza al-sukkiyya fī al-bāb fayteq"

[Al-A'sha's verse: "wa-lā budda min jārin yujīzu sabīlahā / kamā jawwaza al-sukkī fī al-bāb fayteq"], by al-A'sha, describing a desert wasteland in which the wild ass, having been separated from the tribe of Banū 'Ukāẓ, as will come shortly. He says: one who wishes to cross it must have a neighbour, that is, one close to it who helps the traveller to traverse its path. "Jāzahu yajūzuhu" means he traversed it; "ajāzahu yujīzuhu" means he caused it to be traversed; and likewise "jawwazahu yujawwizuhu," with the doubled letter, in both cases. Al-sukkī: the nail, from "al-sakk," which is the riveting and nailing of a door. Al-fayteq: the carpenter, because he splits the wood with the nail. It is narrated as "kamā salaka al-sukkī," meaning: he is not counted among the guides, who pierces it through as the carpenter drives the nail into the door.

He used the past tense to indicate that the comparison is familiar to the listener.

"Fa-atba'ahum": then he overtook them, that is, reached them. It is said: "tabi'tuhu ḥattā atba'tuhu." Al-Hasan recited "wa-'adwan" [Note: in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "ʿadā ʿadwan wa-ʿudwan wa-ʿadā'an." Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 93:

﴿Mubawwa'a sidq﴾ (a dwelling of truth): a good, pleasing abode, and it is Egypt and the Levant (al-Sham). ﴿So they did not differ concerning their religion, nor did they split into factions regarding it, except after knowledge had come to them﴾: they had only fallen into division after they had read the Torah and acquired knowledge of the religion of truth, and steadfastness upon it and unity of word had been incumbent upon them, and they knew that disagreement concerning it leads to dispersion from it.

It is also said: it refers to knowledge of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the disagreement of the Children of Israel, who are the People of the Book, over his description and attributes, and whether he is the one or not. ﴿After knowledge and clear proof had come to them that he is the one, they did not doubt concerning him.﴾ As God Most High said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons.﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verses 94–95:

If you ask: How could He say to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾, alongside His saying about the disbelievers, ﴿And indeed they are in doubt about it, suspicious﴾? [Mahmud said: "If you ask, how did He say to him, peace be upon him, ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, alongside His saying about the disbelievers, ﴿And indeed they are in doubt about it, suspicious﴾ ... etc.?" Ahmad said: If this commentator had said that the negation of doubt from him, peace be upon him, is a preparation (tawti'ah) for His command to him to ask, so that his proof would be established against those who are asked, not so that he would gain knowledge from their answers, given the greater clarity of the disavowal in His saying to him, ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾, where He commanded both the asking and the answering, it would have been more upright and safer. And Allah knows best.] I say: There is a great difference between His saying ﴿And indeed they are in doubt about it, suspicious﴾, which affirms doubt for them by way of emphasis and affirmation, and His saying ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, which carries the meaning of supposition and illustration, as if it were said: If doubt should happen to you, for instance, and Satan should cast confusion into you by way of supposition, ﴿then ask those who read the Book﴾. The meaning is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned first the Children of Israel, who are the readers of the Book, and described them as having received knowledge, because the matter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is written in their Torah and Gospel, and they recognize him as they recognize their own sons. He wished to affirm their knowledge of the soundness of the Qur'an and the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and to emphasize that. So He said: If doubt should befall you, by supposition and assumption. The way of one whom a doubt has troubled in religion is to hasten to resolve it and remove it, either by returning to the principles and proofs of the religion, or by discussing with the scholars who point to the truth. So ask the scholars of the People of the Book, meaning: they have such comprehensive knowledge of the soundness of what was sent down to you, and of its evidence, that they are fit to be consulted by one like you, let alone by others. The purpose is to describe the rabbis as firmly grounded in knowledge of the soundness of what was sent down to the Messenger of Allah, not to describe the Messenger of Allah as being in doubt about it. Then He said: ﴿Certainly the truth has come to you from your Lord﴾, meaning: it has been established for you by clear signs and decisive proofs that what has come to you is the truth, in which there is no room for dispute. ﴿So do not be among the doubters, and do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah﴾, meaning: remain steadfast and persist in what you are upon, the negation of doubt from you and the denial of the signs of Allah. It is also permissible that this be in the manner of stirring up and inciting, like His saying ﴿So do not be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾, and ﴿Let them not turn you away from the signs of Allah after they have been sent down to you﴾, and for the increase of steadfastness and protection. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said when it was revealed: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask; rather I testify that it is the truth." [Abd al-Razzaq narrated it, and from his route al-Tabari, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning this verse, who said: "It has reached us that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'I do not doubt and I do not ask.'"] And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "No, by Allah, he did not doubt for the blink of an eye, nor did he ask any of them." It has also been said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was addressed while the intended meaning is the address to his community, and its meaning is: If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, like His saying ﴿And We sent down to you a clear light﴾. It has also been said: the address is to the listener, from among those for whom doubt is possible, like the Arabs' saying: "If your brother is mighty, then humble yourself." It has also been said: "in" (in) is for negation, meaning: "You were not in doubt, so ask," that is: We do not command you to ask because you are doubting, but so that you may increase in certainty, just as Abraham, peace be upon him, increased in certainty by witnessing the revival of the dead. And it was read: ﴿ask those who read the Books﴾.

Then why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it, before the vision of punishment, while obligation still remained, and that repented of disbelief and sincerely adopted faith, rather than delaying as Pharaoh did until he was seized by the throat (the choking at death), whereupon his faith would not benefit him, since it would not be accepted from him because it occurred at a time when choice had ended? Ubayy recited it thus.

And ʿAbd Allah recited: "Why was there not [any town] except the people of Yunus (Jonah)." This is an exception from "town," because what is meant is its inhabitants. It is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), in the sense of: "But the people of Yunus, when they believed..." It is also permissible for it to be a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), with the sentence being in the sense of negation, as if it were said: "No town of the destroyed towns believed except the people of Yunus," and its being in the accusative is the original form of the exception. It was also read in the nominative as a substitution (badal); this is related from al-Jarmi and al-Kisa'i. It is narrated that Yunus, peace be upon him, was sent to Nineveh in the land of Mosul, and they denied him, so he departed from them in anger. When they lost him, they feared the descent of the punishment, so they put on woolen garments and cried out for forty nights. It was also said: Yunus told them, "Your term is forty nights." They said, "If we see the signs of destruction, we will believe in you." When thirty-five nights had passed, the sky clouded over with a black, terrifying cloud that emitted a thick smoke, then descended until it enveloped their city and blackened their rooftops. They put on woolen garments and went out to the open ground, themselves, their women, their children, and their animals, and they separated the women from the children, and the animals from their young, so they yearned for one another, and the voices and wailing rose. They displayed faith and repentance and humbled themselves, so God had mercy on them and removed the punishment from them. That day was the Day of ʿAshura, a Friday. It is related from Ibn Masʿud that their repentance went so far that they returned the wrongful takings; so much so that a man would pull out a stone on which the foundation of his building had been laid and return it. It was also said: they went out to a shaykh from among the remnants of their scholars and said, "The punishment has descended upon us; what do you think?" He said to them, "Say: 'O Living when there is no living, O Living who gives life to the dead, O Living, there is no god but You.'" They said it, and it was removed from them. It is related from al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad: they said, "O God, our sins have grown great and magnificent, and You are greater than them and more magnificent. Deal with us as You are worthy of, and do not deal with us as we are worthy of."

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 99:**

﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ رَبُّكَ﴾ "And if your Lord had willed," in the sense of willing by compulsion [[His saying "willing by compulsion" is the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). They held that God is obligated to do what is good and best (al-salah wa al-aslah), and the belief of all people is better. But the verse contradicts their doctrine, so they said: God willed the belief of all people with a will of granting choice (irādat takhyir) to His servants, so the willed outcome did not necessarily occur. Had He willed with a will of compulsion (irādat ijbar), it would have occurred. Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community) did not make anything obligatory upon God. The necessary occurrence of what He wills does not contradict the choice of the servants, because they have acquisition (kasb) in their voluntary acts, even though the true agent of those acts is God, as is established in the discussion of tawhid (divine oneness). (ʿ)]] and by compulsion and coercion [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The meaning is the will of compulsion and coercion." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This is an insertion of Mu'tazilism stealthily, and a mixing of falsehood with truth deceptively. When he knew that the verse implies the non-willing of God for the belief of creation, by the universal wording, and that He willed that only for those who believe and not for those who disbelieve, since the implication of "law lā" is prohibition, and this was a refutation of his corrupt creed, for they claim that God willed belief from all the people of the earth, yet only some of them believed, he began to distort the will of belief into the will of compulsion and coercion, so that it would be complete for him that the will stated in the verse did not occur. However, we agree with him that God did not compel creation nor nullify their choice; rather He commanded them to believe and created for them choice and intention. This, as you see, does not count as interpretation (ta'wil). Rather it is more deserving of negation (ta'til), so it is obligatory to reject it and to affirm the apparent meaning as it is. We seek refuge in God from the deviation of Satan and his misguidance, and God is the Granter of success.]] ﴿لَآمَنَ مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ كُلُّهُمْ﴾ "those on earth would have believed, all of them," in the sense of encompassing and including totality, ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ "together," gathered upon belief, unanimous in it, not differing about it. Do you not see His saying: ﴿أَفَأَنْتَ تُكْرِهُ النَّاسَ﴾ "Then would you compel the people?" meaning: it is He alone who is able to compel them and force them to belief, not you. The placing of the pronoun (ism) before the interrogative particle (harf al-istifham) is to inform that compulsion is possible and within capacity, but the matter concerns who the one compelling is. And there is none but Him alone, with none sharing in it, because He is the One able to act upon their hearts so that they are forced to belief at that point, and that is not within the power of human beings.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 100:

"And it is not for any soul [to believe] except by the permission of Allah" — meaning, of the souls that He knows will believe — "except by the permission of Allah," i.e., by His facilitating it, which is the bestowing of favours (alta'if). "And He places defilement upon those who do not use their reason." He contrasts permission with defilement (rijs), which is abandonment (khidhlan) [[His saying "which is abandonment": interpreting rijs as khidhlan is according to the school of the Mu'tazila; according to the Ahl al-Sunna there is no need to interpret it. (Gh.)]]. The soul whose belief is known is contrasted with "those who do not use their reason," who are those who persist in disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not understand﴾. He called abandonment "rijs," and it is the punishment, because it is its cause. It is also read "ar-rijz" with a zay. And it is read "wa-najʿalu" with a nun.

What is in the heavens and the earth ﴿of signs and lessons﴾? ﴿And signs and warnings will not avail﴾, that is, the signs, the warnings, the messengers who warn, or the admonitions, ﴿for a people who do not believe﴾, whose faith is not to be expected. They are the ones who do not use their reason. It is also recited as ﴿wa-ma yughni﴾ with the ya', and "mā" is then either a negation particle or an interrogative.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 102–103:

"Days" of those who passed away before them: the events of God Most High concerning them, just as it is said "the days of the Arabs" (meaning their battles).

Then We shall save Our messengers: this is coordinated with a deleted statement, indicated by His words: "except like the days of those who passed away before them." It is as if it were said: We destroy the nations, then We save Our messengers, by way of narrating past conditions.

And those who believed: and whoever believed with them. Likewise: "We shall save the believers" — with that same kind of saving — "We shall save the believers" from among you, and We destroy the polytheists.

And "upon Us" is a parenthetical clause, meaning: that is incumbent upon Us as a binding obligation. It has been read as nunajji (with doubled jim, intensive form).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 102–103:

"Days" of those who passed away before them: the events of God Most High concerning them, just as it is said "the days of the Arabs" (meaning their battles).

Then We shall save Our messengers: this is coordinated with a deleted statement, indicated by His words: "except like the days of those who passed away before them." It is as if it were said: We destroy the nations, then We save Our messengers, by way of narrating past conditions.

And those who believed: and whoever believed with them. Likewise: "We shall save the believers" — with that same kind of saving — "We shall save the believers" from among you, and We destroy the polytheists.

And "upon Us" is a parenthetical clause, meaning: that is incumbent upon Us as a binding obligation. It has been read as nunajji (with doubled jim, intensive form).

O people, [O people of Makkah], if you are in doubt about my religion, its soundness and its correctness, then here is my religion: listen to its description, present it to your minds, and examine it with an eye of fairness, so that you may know that it is a religion into which doubt has no entry. It is this: I do not worship the stones that you worship besides Him who is your God and your Creator. ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾. He described Him by causing death (tawaffi) only to show them that He is the one truly deserving to be feared and guarded against, so that He alone is worshipped rather than that which has no power over anything. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾. That is, Allah has commanded me to this, through the intellect He has placed within me and through what He has revealed to me in His Book.

It has been said: the meaning is, if you are in doubt about my religion and about what I am upon (whether I will remain upon it or abandon it and agree with you), then do not entertain vain notions and do not doubt my affair, cut off the hope of your desires, and know that I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah, and I do not choose misguidance over guidance, like His saying: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾ [109:1–2]. ﴿I have been commanded to be among...﴾ Its original form is: "bi-an akuna" (that I be), so the preposition was omitted. This omission may be of the regular kind, which is the omission of prepositions before "inna" and "an," or it may be of the irregular kind, as in His saying: "Amartuka al-khayr fa-sda' bima tu'mar" (I have commanded you good, so proclaim what you are commanded).

I say: the coordination of His words "and that I should establish" (wa an aqim) upon "that I should be" (an akūna) is problematic, because "an" (that) must be either the "an" of expressing speech (al-'ibara), or the "an" which with the verb forms a verbal noun (masdar). It is not valid for it to be the "an" of expressing speech, even though the command contains the meaning of saying, because its coordination with the relative-type (mawsula) "an" refuses that. And the claim that it is a relative-type "an" like the first does not agree with the form of the command, aqim, because the relative clause (sila) must be a sentence capable of truth and falsehood.

I answer: Sibawayh permitted that "an" be followed by a command and a prohibition, and he compared that to their saying: "You are the one who does," in the second person, because the purpose is to link it to what it is with in the sense of a verbal noun. Command and prohibition indicate the verbal noun in a way other verbs do not: "Establish your face" (aqim wajhaka), "Be upright" (istaqim), "Turn to it," and "Do not turn right or left." And "hanifan" (upright, in pure monotheism) is a state (hal) of "the religion" (al-din), or of "the face" (al-wajh).

If you do that, then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers. Its meaning is: if you call upon other than Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you, then he has referred to that by the verb "do" (fa'alta) for the sake of brevity. "Then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers" (fa-innaka idhan min al-zalimin): "idhan" is the response to a condition and an answer to an implied question, as if a questioner had asked about the consequence of worshipping idols. He was described as among the wrongdoers because there is no greater wrongdoing than shirk (association of partners with Allah), ﴿Indeed, association of partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong.﴾

Having forbidden the worship of idols and described them as unable to benefit or harm, He (Exalted and Majestic is He) then states that Allah is the One who harms and benefits: if He afflicts you with harm, none can remove it except Him alone, not any single person, so how could a lifeless idol that has no awareness do so? Likewise, if He wills good for you, none can withhold from you what He wills of His bounty and kindness, so how could idols? He is therefore the one deserving that worship be directed to Him rather than to them. This is more eloquent than His saying: ﴿If Allah intends harm for me, can they remove His harm? Or if He intends mercy for me, can they withhold His mercy?﴾

If you ask: why is touching (al-mass) mentioned in one of the two, and willing (al-iradah) in the second? I answer: it is as though he intended to mention both matters together: willing and afflicting, in each of harm and good, and that there is no one who can turn back what He wills of either of them, nor remove what He afflicts with of either of them. So he concisely stated touching, which is affliction, in one, and willing in the other, so that what was mentioned indicates what was omitted. Moreover, he has mentioned affliction with good in His saying, ﴿He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants﴾, and what is meant by the will (al-mashi'ah) here is the will of what is beneficial (mashi'at al-maslahah).

Surely the truth has come to you from your Lord, so no excuse remains for you, and there is no proof left against Allah. Whoever chooses guidance and follows the truth, the benefit of his choosing accrues only to himself; and whoever prefers error, the harm falls only upon himself. The particles "lam" (ل, for) and "ʿalā" (على, against) indicate the meanings of benefit and harm. The matter is left to them after the truth has been made clear and the pretexts removed. In this there is an exhortation to prefer guidance and to cast aside error. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: not a keeper entrusted with your affairs, nor one to compel you to what I desire. ﴿I am only a bringer of good news and a warner.﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 10, verse 109:

﴿And be patient until Allah judges, and He is the best of judges.﴾ That is, be patient with their call, bear their harm and their turning away, until Allah gives you victory over them and dominance.

It is narrated that when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered the Ansar and said: "Indeed you will find, after me, favoritism (athara), so be patient until you meet me." [[Al-Tha'labi narrated it from Anas without a chain. The story mentioned is agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayhi) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd in the course of a longer narration, and from the hadith of Usayd ibn Hudayr, in which there is no mention of this verse being the cause; rather its cause was the division of the spoils of Hunayn.]] That is: I was commanded in this verse to be patient with what the disbelievers inflicted upon me, so I was patient; you too, be patient with what the oppressive rulers impose upon you. Anas said: "So we did not be patient."

It is also narrated that Abu Qatada stayed behind from welcoming Mu'awiya when he came to Madina, while the Ansar had gone out to receive him. Then he entered upon him later, and Mu'awiya said to him: "What is wrong with you that you did not welcome us?" He said: "We had no mounts." He said: "Then where are the camels for carrying water (nawadih)?" He said: "We slaughtered them in your pursuit and your father's pursuit on the day of Badr. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said: 'O assembly of the Ansar, indeed you will meet after me with favoritism (athara).'" Mu'awiya said: "And what did he say?" He said: "He said, 'So be patient until you meet me.'" He said: "Then be patient." He said: "Then we shall be patient."

So Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan [[Narrated by Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and through him al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, from Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Ibn Aqil, that when Mu'awiya came to Madina, Abu Qatada al-Ansari met him. Mu'awiya said: "All the people welcomed us except you, O assembly of the Ansar; what prevents you from welcoming me?" He said: "We had no mounts." Mu'awiya said: "Then where are the camels?" Abu Qatada said: "We slaughtered them in your pursuit and your father's pursuit on the day of Badr." Then Abu Qatada said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed you will see, after me, favoritism.'" Mu'awiya said: "What then commands you?" He said: "We were commanded to be patient until we meet him." He said: "Then be patient until you meet him." When this reached Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan, he said — and he mentioned the two verses — and he said: "O Commander of the Faithful."]] said:

Verily, let it be conveyed to Mu'awiya ibn Harb, / commander of the wrongdoers, the statement of my words (nathā kalāmī),

That we are patient, so wait for you / until the Day of Mutual Loss (al-taghabun) and dispute (al-khisam).

[[Said by Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan when Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan ibn Harb entered Madina, the Ansar welcomed him, and Abu Qatada stayed behind, then entered upon him and said: "What is wrong with you that you stayed behind?" He said: "We had no mounts." He said: "Then where are the camels for carrying water?" He said: "We slaughtered them in your pursuit and your father's pursuit on the day of Badr, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O assembly of the Ansar, you will meet after me with favoritism.'"
